title: Digital Exploration of Interior Design (1)

jokes.text: Dean Pelton struggles to cut the ribbon with ceremonial scissors, then resorts to using his teeth, delivering 'The legitimate!' twice with increasing absurdity
jokes.setup: Dean grandly declares this a historic day for Greendale entering 'the realm of the legitimate' as he attempts a ribbon-cutting ceremony
jokes.punchline: He can't even cut the ribbon properly and uses his teeth, then keeps repeating 'The legitimate!' as if the word itself is a proclamation
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy for the Dean — his aspirational pomposity undercut immediately by physical incompetence. 'The legitimate!' as a repeated exclamation is a funny verbal tic. The image of a dean gnawing a ribbon is strong. Character integration is high because this joke only works for Dean Pelton.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Thank you all for coming to this momentous occasion—the opening of Greendale's very own Subway restaurant, a symbol of our institution's commitment to legitimate dining options and student wellness.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Now, if I could just—

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: These scissors are... they're not cooperating. Hold on.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: One moment, please. The ribbon is—it's caught. It's very caught.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I have operated scissors before. Many times. I'm very capable.

jokes.text: Dean repeating 'The legitimate! The legitimate!' with apparent genuine excitement as the ceremony collapses
jokes.setup: Dean is celebrating Greendale entering 'the realm of the legitimate'
jokes.punchline: He keeps ecstatically repeating the word while actively failing to perform a basic task, making the word ring increasingly hollow
jokes.explanation: The repetition escalates the irony — the more enthusiastically Dean says 'legitimate,' the more illegitimate the moment becomes. Solid character work but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, I'm just so proud that our little sandwich shop inspired this beautiful Subway. I mean, when I opened my doors, nobody believed in the dream. But look at this! *gestures around* They believed in it so much, they decided to do it themselves. With their money. And their locations. And their corporate infrastructure.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'That should be my sandwich shop. It was my idea to put one there.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is reacting to the new Subway opening at Greendale
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately makes it about herself and her displaced entrepreneurial dream, delivered with quiet indignation
jokes.explanation: Solid character-specific beat that establishes the episode's B-plot. Shirley's entrepreneurial grievance is a known character trait so the joke pays off on recognition. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm staying at a sleep study for a while. They're paying me to sleep, which is basically my dream job. Well, my dream job would be sleeping, but this is pretty close.

jokes.text: Troy explains their homelessness: 'They're tenting our building for termites, so we're homeless.' Then immediately: 'I'm staying in the sleep study lab. All I have to do is wake up every three hours and go... and I get two credits.'
jokes.setup: Troy explains he, Annie, and someone else are 'displaced' due to building fumigation
jokes.punchline: He's solved homelessness by living in a sleep lab — a school-credit-bearing solution — and the ellipsis implies he makes a funny noise or gesture every three hours
jokes.explanation: Troy's cheerful obliviousness to his own absurd situation is well-executed. The implied sound/gesture he performs every three hours is a visual gag embedded in a subtitle gap — clever structural use of the transcript format. Greendale-specific logic (getting credits for weird activities) adds institutional comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, didn't you guys just build a fort like last week?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That was a pillow fort.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is a blanket fort.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Completely different.

jokes.text: Abed/Troy announce plans for a 'super awesome pillow fort.' Jeff says 'Kind of repeating yourselves, aren't you?' Troy: 'That was a blanket fort. This will be a pillow fort. Way more difficult, way better.'
jokes.setup: Jeff points out the group already did a fort-related episode (Season 2's 'Pillows and Blankets' predecessor), calling them out for self-repetition
jokes.punchline: Troy's pedantic distinction between blanket and pillow forts — delivered with complete sincerity — is both the in-universe retort AND the show's meta-defense of doing a fort episode again
jokes.explanation: This is exceptionally well-constructed meta-comedy. Jeff's critique IS the audience's critique, and Troy's sincere rebuttal IS the writers' sincere rebuttal — both simultaneously. The fact that the distinction between blanket and pillow forts becomes the entire thematic engine of the episode gives this retroactive weight. High character integration: Jeff is the cynic, Troy is the true believer. Rewatch bonus because viewers re-watching know Troy is completely right.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Difficulty is inherently valuable. It builds character.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So if I made you eat broken glass, that would build your character?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's different.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: How? It's difficult. By your logic, the more glass you eat, the better a person you become.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You're twisting my words.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm just following your philosophy to its logical conclusion. Maybe we should all just walk into traffic. That's pretty difficult.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'My brain starts getting weird this time of night.' Jeff: 'It's 10:00 a.m.' Pierce: 'You're welcome.'
jokes.setup: Pierce makes a vague comment about his brain getting weird
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects him that it's only 10 AM; Pierce responds 'You're welcome' — a non-sequitur that implies he's taking credit for something, probably the information itself, in complete disconnect from the conversation
jokes.explanation: Perfect three-beat rhythm. Pierce's 'You're welcome' is hilariously wrong — he takes credit for being corrected, or perhaps for the time of day, or simply has no idea what's happening. The joke is entirely in that non-sequitur pivot. Very economical and Pierce-specific: his disconnect from reality is played deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's late, I'm not thinking straight.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, it's 9 AM.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

jokes.text: 'All difficult things are better, like carrying a disease or holding in a fart right now.'
jokes.setup: Troy is making the case that difficulty equals quality
jokes.punchline: His examples escalate from the mundane to the absurd ('carrying a disease') and then immediately to the present-tense physical confession ('holding in a fart right now'), which turns abstract philosophy into immediate bodily reality
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The structure is perfect: abstract philosophical claim → first example (odd but defensible) → second example that is both absurd AND immediate and confessional, completely collapsing the grandeur of the argument. Troy's childlike sincerity in confessing he is currently holding in a fart mid-speech is perfect character integration. High quotability — this line travels. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, actually, the course designation is quite important. It reflects the academic rigor and subject matter. For instance, I'm taking PTSD 101.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... not a real class code.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It stands for 'Philosophical Theories and Systemic Dynamics.' It's perfectly legitimate.

jokes.text: Pierce says 'Aha!' responding to Shirley's fart-holding comment, suggesting he interpreted it as a confession or signal
jokes.setup: Troy confesses to holding in a fart
jokes.punchline: Pierce's immediate 'Aha!' — either he's reacting to Troy's gas, smelled something, or is making an oddly triumphant non-sequitur — lands as a perfect reaction beat
jokes.explanation: One word carrying a solid laugh through pure timing and ambiguity. Economy score is near-perfect — maximum comedy per syllable. The joke depends entirely on delivery and Pierce's specific obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We have a new student joining us today. Please welcome our newest Greendale student.

dialogue.speaker: New Student
dialogue.line: Thank you. My name is Corporate Synergy LLC.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Wonderful! Welcome to Greendale, Corporate Synergy LLC.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Wait, that's your actual legal name?

dialogue.speaker: Corporate Synergy LLC
dialogue.line: Yes. I was born a limited liability corporation. My parents wanted me to have all the legal protections of a business entity.

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Corporate Synergy LLC
dialogue.line: Actually, thanks to Citizens United, I have more constitutional rights than you do.

jokes.text: The concept of 'corpohumanization' — a legal process by which a corporation becomes a human being named after the company
jokes.setup: Subway corporation has enrolled as a student; the group demands an explanation
jokes.punchline: The term 'corpohumanization' is delivered deadpan as 'groundbreaking but surprisingly legal,' as if the only surprising part is the legality, not the fundamental horror of the concept
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical concept that earns its score. 'Corpohumanization' is a genuinely original coinage that skewers Citizens United/corporate personhood in a way that is both funny and intellectually pointed. The qualifier 'surprisingly legal' does heavy lifting — it validates the audience's disbelief while also being the precise absurdist deflation. This is the episode's central satirical premise delivered economically. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is exactly what's wrong with corporate personhood! A massive corporation literally walking around, exploiting workers, destroying the environment—

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: I'm just here to make sandwiches.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: And another thing—how tall are you? Like, seven feet?

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Come on, Subway, there is no way you're 5'10".'
jokes.setup: Subway has just explained the concept of corpohumanization and introduced himself as a legal human
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response ignores every philosophical and legal horror of what just happened and zeroes in on the most trivial possible objection: the guy's listed height
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff Winger move: confronted with something that should provoke moral outrage, he focuses on the petty and self-referential. The joke works on two levels — it's a vain height complaint from Jeff AND a perfect deflation of the absurd premise. High character integration because this is exactly Jeff's brand of shallow narcissism. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, if Subway is a corporate person, does that mean it has civic rights?

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: I suppose technically, yes.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So you can vote?

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: Well, I'm only 50 years old.

dialogue.speaker: Group
dialogue.line: Aww...

jokes.text: Annie asks 'So you can vote?' and Subway replies 'Actually, no, because technically I'm only a week old.' Then: 'Aww.'
jokes.setup: Annie asks the logical civic question about whether Subway can vote
jokes.punchline: The voting question is answered not by legal status but by age — Subway is literally only a week old as a person — followed by an involuntary sympathetic 'Aww' from someone in the group, treating a corporate entity like a baby
jokes.explanation: Elegant two-beat joke. Annie's question is the straight-man pivot that sets up an unexpected axis — not legality but age. 'Aww' is the perfect button, showing the group unconsciously humanizing a corporation. The logic is airtight within the absurd premise. Good structural craft.

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not actually a student here?

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: No, I'm in the military. I have to serve my country.

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

jokes.text: Subway: 'I'm here to hang out, take weird classes, and party as hearty as my morality clause allows.' Then does the Subway slogan 'Eat fresh?' as a greeting, which another character reciprocates.
jokes.setup: Subway is trying to present himself as a normal, relatable student
jokes.punchline: 'Party as hearty as my morality clause allows' perfectly encapsulates the horror of corporate personhood — this 'human' has contractual limits on how much fun he can have. The 'Eat fresh?' handshake is a brand slogan becoming a social greeting, used completely sincerely.
jokes.explanation: Two strong jokes packed together. 'Morality clause allows' is sharp corporate satire. 'Eat fresh' as a sincere greeting/handshake is an excellent running gag seed — it will recur throughout the episode each time Subway exits a scene, gaining power with repetition.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, there's a student lounge? How did I not know about this?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You missed orientation, Jeff. There were a lot of activities.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How many activities could there possibly be?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, there was the welcome mixer, the campus scavenger hunt, the diversity fair, the club showcase, the midnight dodgeball tournament, the synchronized swimming exhibition, and the ceremonial lighting of the dean on fire.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, what was that last one?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm kidding about that one.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're kidding about one of them?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Wow, did you know Greendale students are technically in the army reserves? Let's say a little prayer for peace.'
jokes.setup: The group has just met Subway and is processing his existence
jokes.punchline: Pierce completely ignores the corporate personhood horror show and pivots to an entirely unrelated non-sequitur piece of Greendale trivia, then immediately calls for a prayer — implying violence is likely
jokes.explanation: Pierce's non-sequitur humor at its functional best — the pivot is complete and the prayer for peace implies he anticipates catastrophe. Greendale institutional absurdism (students in army reserves) is a reliable comedy vein. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, so if they won't let me bring Mr. Whiskers into the sleep study, I'll just have to get creative. I'm thinking I tape him to the underside of my mattress, but not too tight because he needs to breathe. Then I wear an oversized cardigan with deep pockets, and I fill those pockets with smaller stuffed animals as decoys. When they search me, they'll find the decoys and think they've won. But the real prize? Mr. Whiskers will be in a hollowed-out pillow.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I've already measured his dimensions. It's a perfect fit. And if that doesn't work, I have a backup plan involving my bra. I'm not going to explain that part, but let's just say Mr. Whiskers is very small and very important to my REM cycles.

jokes.text: Jeff asks Annie to get him into the sleep study lab: 'I can't think of a better use of my time here than being unconscious.'
jokes.setup: Annie is enthusiastically describing her sleep study arrangement
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames unconsciousness as a positive academic goal — a perfect encapsulation of his anti-effort philosophy toward Greendale
jokes.explanation: Clean character-specific line. Jeff's laziness as a philosophy is well-established, and 'being unconscious' as aspirational is a good compression of that attitude. Not his sharpest line but reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Winter Formal. Spring Fling. Winter Formal II. Spring Fling II: The Flinging. Winter Formal: The Formaling. Spring Fling III: This Time It's Personal. Winter Formal IV: We Mean It This Time. Spring Fling: The Reckoning.

jokes.text: Annie: 'We're only allowed to bring one stuffed animal. I'm bringing Ruthie... but using her pouch to sneak in Nathan.'
jokes.setup: Annie is describing the strict rules of the sleep lab
jokes.punchline: She's already strategizing how to smuggle a second stuffed animal inside the first one — Ruthie is a kangaroo with a pouch. The level of planning and investment in this problem is entirely Annie.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The stuffed animal smuggling operation (with named animals, a kangaroo chosen specifically for her pouch, a secondary stuffed animal named Nathan) reveals Annie's compulsive rule-bending-within-rules personality perfectly. The specificity of 'Ruthie' and 'Nathan' elevates it from a generic joke about Annie being uptight into something genuinely charming and specific. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so you guys actually saved Garrett?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't know.

jokes.text: Jeff discovers he has a locker he's never used: 'Wait, since when do we have lockers?' Annie: 'Since registration day, 2009.' Jeff: 'Did you skip the Preorientation Freshman Welcome Seminar and Diversity Fire Circle?' Jeff: 'Are you saying I've had a locker here for 2 1/2 years?'
jokes.setup: Jeff is walking the halls and notices lockers for the first time
jokes.punchline: He has apparently attended this school for 2.5 years without ever attending orientation or noticing the lockers. The 'Diversity Fire Circle' is a perfect Greendale-specific absurdist detail.
jokes.explanation: Good institutional comedy anchored in character. Jeff's obliviousness to basic campus infrastructure after 2.5 years is both funny and plot-functional (it sets up the Kim storyline). 'Diversity Fire Circle' is a great Greendale course/event name — specific enough to be believable, absurd enough to be funny. Annie's precise recall ('registration day, 2009') is a nice character contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Garrett! Thank God, we got you out of there. Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: I'm fine, I'm fine. Though I'm not sure 'rescued' is the right word.

jokes.text: Jeff opens his locker and finds years of accumulated flyers: 'Halloween dance.' 'Post-Halloween dance.' 'Dance contest.' 'Contest dance.'
jokes.setup: Jeff opens a locker he hasn't touched in 2.5 years
jokes.punchline: The progression 'Dance contest' → 'Contest dance' — just the words reversed — implies Greendale ran out of ideas and started recycling event names with minimal effort
jokes.explanation: Smart escalating list joke. The first three are plausible, the fourth ('Contest dance' — literally just the previous two words swapped) is the punchline, implying institutional decay and creative bankruptcy. Well-structured list comedy with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I just said something stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Gesundheit.

jokes.text: Jeff finds a 'Save Garrett' flyer. 'What's wrong with Garrett?' 'Nothing now. We saved him.'
jokes.setup: Jeff finds a flyer among his old locker contents calling for saving Garrett
jokes.punchline: Annie's completely flat 'Nothing now. We saved him.' — delivered as if 'saving Garrett' was a routine administrative task — is funnier than any explanation would be
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words do enormous comedic work. The joke is entirely in what's NOT explained. The phrase 'We saved him' has a heroic grandeur that Annie delivers with complete casualness, implying this was just another Tuesday at Greendale. The ambiguity of what Garrett needed saving from is funnier than any answer.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what? Crowd mentality is a real problem. People just go along with whatever everyone else is doing without thinking for themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Like, do snakes even travel in herds? I don't think they do... actually, I'm not sure. Do they?

jokes.text: Jeff opens what appears to be a photo of 'saved' Garrett. 'Aah!' — 'Wait, that's saved Garrett?'
jokes.setup: 'We saved him' has just been delivered with cheerful confidence
jokes.punchline: Jeff's horror-movie scream followed by 'Wait, that's SAVED Garrett?' implies the saved version is still alarming — the before version must have been catastrophic
jokes.explanation: Strong visual/reaction joke that works even without seeing the image. The structure — Annie's confident 'we saved him,' then Jeff's scream, then 'that's SAVED Garrett?' — creates a three-beat escalation. The unseen image is funnier than any image could be. Good callback to Garrett as the school's lovable disaster character.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I came up with the perfect name for my advice column: 'Dear Filtration.'

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why 'Filtration'?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Because I filter out the bad advice and let the good advice flow through, like a water filter.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh. I thought it was just a weird way to spell 'Dear Abby.'

jokes.text: Jeff finds what he thinks is a love letter. 'Oh, it's probably one of many.' Then: 'Oh, no. This is a hate letter.'
jokes.setup: Jeff finds an envelope in his locker and assumes it's a love letter — 'probably one of many,' he says with complete confidence
jokes.punchline: It's a hate letter. The confident narcissism of 'probably one of many' makes the reversal land harder.
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection setup. Jeff's 'probably one of many' is the comedic investment that pays off when the reversal hits. The structure is well-practiced but executed crisply. 'One of many' is the key — it inflates the expectation so the deflation hits harder.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You could probably get him to do anything. You know, with your... way of communicating.

jokes.text: The hate letter reads: 'Dear Jeff, this might come as a shock to someone who thinks he's God's gift to the world, but you're actually an inconsiderate jerk. Kim.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is reading his 'hate letter' aloud
jokes.punchline: The letter is perfectly calibrated Jeff criticism — 'someone who thinks he's God's gift to the world' is exactly right — but then it's signed with a simple 'Kim,' as if one devastating sentence was enough
jokes.explanation: The letter works because it's accurate — Jeff IS exactly the person described — and the economy of Kim's insult (one sentence, one sign-off) has the finality of a verdict. Sets up the Kim storyline effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've got a grappling hook, night vision goggles, a poisoned dart gun... and my penis. That's the deadliest weapon of all.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I don't know, and clearly she doesn't know me.' Then someone sneezes (implied), Jeff says 'Gesundheit,' and is told 'I didn't sneeze.'
jokes.setup: Jeff defensively declares Kim doesn't know him
jokes.punchline: He hears something that sounds like a sneeze and immediately social-graces it; when corrected, the implied pause — the unspoken 'then what did I hear?' — is funnier than any explanation
jokes.explanation: Light gag, mostly serving as a breather between beats. The implication is some bodily sound other than a sneeze was made (connecting back to Troy's fart joke), but the connection is thin. Functional but low-craft.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not going to do some seduction plan. That's manipulative and gross.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Come on, Britta. It's not that bad.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Not that bad? Jeff, I have a very specific, elaborate fantasy about being a high-end escort in Manhattan with my own brownstone and a security detail, and I'm not going to compromise that by actually manipulating people.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Look at these idiots. Cattle, sheep... other animals that travel in herds. I want to say snakes.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is scornfully watching students line up for Subway
jokes.punchline: 'I want to say snakes' — Pierce confidently begins a herd-animal metaphor and then undermines it completely with his own ignorance of basic animal behavior. Snakes are not herd animals.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce line. The setup is a pompous cultural critique; the punchline is Pierce revealing he doesn't know that snakes are solitary. The 'I want to say' hedge is perfect — it's not confident ignorance but tentative ignorance, which is somehow worse and funnier. Character integration is very high: Pierce would absolutely try to make this speech. Very economical — the joke is exactly as long as it needs to be.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: This is just a coupon for Bed Bath & Beyond.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: But I'll take it.

jokes.text: Britta: 'I totally predicted this in my High School newspaper column, Britta Unfiltered.' Pierce: 'Unfiltered. I get it.' Britta: 'Get what?'
jokes.setup: Britta is claiming prescient political awareness via her high school newspaper column called 'Britta Unfiltered'
jokes.punchline: Pierce claims to 'get it,' implying a cigarette joke (unfiltered cigarettes). Britta's 'Get what?' reveals she named herself after cigarettes without knowing it, OR that Pierce is making a connection she never intended.
jokes.explanation: Sharp three-beat joke. The column name reads as self-important political journalism; Pierce reads it as a cigarette reference; Britta has no idea what he's even talking about. The punchline is Britta's obliviousness — she can't even parse the joke about herself. Very economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh man, I can't believe we're meeting actual Guinness World Record holders!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, the guy with the longest fingernails hasn't trimmed them since 2003. He can't wipe. He pays someone to do it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: ...What?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not a record. That's a cry for help.

jokes.text: Pierce to Britta: 'You're a, uh, progressive woman of a more... liberated looseness.' — suggesting she should seduce Subway for corporate espionage
jokes.setup: Pierce is suggesting Britta could get close to Subway and find dirt on him
jokes.punchline: 'Liberated looseness' is a spectacularly awkward euphemism for promiscuity, delivered with Pierce's particular brand of well-meaning-but-offensive framing
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — the specific phrase 'liberated looseness' is doing a lot of work. It's the kind of euphemism only Pierce would construct: quasi-feminist framing wrapped around a sexist request. Character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: You're like Laverne and Shirley. And you're like... Reggie.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Who's Reggie?

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Corporate espionage. I like it. Microphones hidden in lipstick. Lipstick hidden in microphones. And the deadliest weapon of them all... The penis flytrap.'
jokes.setup: Britta has just agreed the espionage plan sounds interesting
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from spy-movie clichés (microphone in lipstick) to its own inversion (lipstick in microphone, which makes no sense) to 'the penis flytrap' — a term so bizarre and specific it derails the entire conversation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation structure is immaculate: a sensible spy cliché, then its nonsensical inversion (you can't put lipstick inside a microphone in any useful way), then the full detonation of 'the penis flytrap.' The term is memorable, visual, and horrifying in ways the show wisely doesn't explain. The list structure earns the final term — without the first two beats building the rhythm, the punchline wouldn't land as hard. Shirley's 'Okay! This conversation is over' is the perfect button. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Reggie can do anything! He's incredibly talented and loyal.

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sure he is. But you see, Troy, what matters isn't what Reggie can do—it's what I allow him to do.

jokes.text: Britta: 'I am not a whore, and not that I've done the math, but if I were, I'd be the super classy kind that gets flown to Dubai to stay in an underwater hotel.'
jokes.setup: Britta is pushing back against the implication that she should seduce Subway
jokes.punchline: She insists she's not a whore — but then can't help specifying exactly what tier of whore she WOULD be, complete with geographic and hospitality details, undermining her own denial completely
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. The joke structure is in two distinct halves that contradict each other — the righteous denial and then the deeply considered hypothetical. 'Not that I've done the math' is the killer qualifier: it acknowledges that she HAS done the math while pretending she hasn't. The specificity of 'Dubai' and 'underwater hotel' is perfect — these are real details that signal she has absolutely thought about this. Character integration is as high as it gets for Britta: her blend of feminist indignation and latent vanity is precisely her. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, Kim is dead?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah, she died last year.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: You know what they say: 'You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.' But what about the shots that take you?

jokes.text: Dean Pelton shows up to investigate the fort permit situation. Troy presents what he claims is a permit, and the Dean realizes: 'This is a coupon for 20% off at Bed Bath and Beyond.'
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy confidently produce 'all the proper permits right here'
jokes.punchline: The permit is a Bed Bath and Beyond coupon — either Troy genuinely confused it for a permit, or he hoped the Dean wouldn't notice
jokes.explanation: Solid but not exceptional. The specific store (Bed Bath and Beyond, relevant to fort-building) is a nice detail. Troy's cheerful confidence in presenting the wrong document is good character work. The joke is functional and gets a laugh but doesn't have the structural elegance of the episode's better material.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Remember when we saved Garrett? Well, he needs saving again.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: I'm fine, actually.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Not from us, Garrett. From life.

jokes.text: Troy wants to build a pillow fort; Abed mentions Shridhar Chillal (the Guinness record holder for longest fingernails). Troy: 'Not interested. I saw him on a talk show. He came off as pretentious.'
jokes.setup: Troy suggests they might meet 'that dude with the curly fingernails' if they win the Guinness record
jokes.punchline: Abed names him (Shridhar Chillal — a real person), and Troy dismisses him not on grounds of irrelevance but on the specific social charge of being 'pretentious' — a judgment apparently formed from one talk show appearance
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising joke. That Abed knows the name 'Shridhar Chillal' is funny on its own (Abed as a repository of arcane information). That Troy has a fully formed negative opinion of this person based on a single talk show appearance — finding him 'pretentious' — is the detonation. The specificity of 'pretentious' applied to a Guinness record fingernail grower is delightfully absurd. Good rewatch value because the name is a real reference.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm here to expose Subway's corporate crimes and shut down your operation.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Employee
dialogue.line: Would you like that six inch or footlong?

jokes.text: Vice Dean Laybourne appears with 'a beard and a ponytail.' Troy: 'You have a beard... and a ponytail.' Laybourne: 'Going through some stuff right now, Troy. Don't worry about it.'
jokes.setup: Vice Dean Laybourne appears in a new location, apparently having undergone a visual transformation
jokes.punchline: 'Going through some stuff right now, Troy. Don't worry about it.' — the Vice Dean of an air conditioning repair school deflects attention from his crisis-beard with the most casual possible non-explanation
jokes.explanation: Good character work for Laybourne — the 'going through some stuff' line is funny precisely because it's delivered by someone who is usually menacingly composed. The mid-life crisis beard/ponytail combo as a visual gag is a reliable comedy trope, but Laybourne's specific delivery elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is just like 1984. Big Brother is watching us.

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's true.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're a sandwich.

jokes.text: Laybourne uses the Inspector Spacetime analogy: Troy = the Inspector (decisive, smart), Abed = Constable Reggie (trusty but... just Reggie). Troy: 'Cool!' — before he's heard the full comparison.
jokes.setup: Laybourne is flattering Troy by comparing him to the Inspector (the star of their favorite show)
jokes.punchline: Troy says 'Cool!' mid-sentence, before Laybourne reveals that Abed is Reggie — the sidekick who gets nothing without the Inspector's permission
jokes.explanation: The 'Cool!' from Troy is perfectly timed — he jumps at the flattery before hearing the manipulation. It also establishes that the Inspector Spacetime comparison is designed to plant a seed of doubt about his friendship with Abed, which pays off later. Good structural setup for the episode's emotional throughline.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My eyesight's not what it used to be.

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: Well, whose is?

jokes.text: Laybourne on Reggie: 'He never really gets to blow the whistle unless the Inspector says it's okay.' Then: 'Less of a friendship, more of a self-centered nerd and his naive, obedient lapdog.'
jokes.setup: Laybourne is using the Inspector/Reggie analogy to suggest Troy is being used by Abed
jokes.punchline: The whistle line is a funny specific detail (Reggie has a whistle but can't use it), but the full reveal — 'self-centered nerd and his naive, obedient lapdog' — is devastatingly blunt after the gentle metaphor
jokes.explanation: The whistle detail is a nice piece of made-up mythology (a constable with a whistle he can't use is a perfect symbol of powerlessness), and the final drop of the metaphor into plain language — 'lapdog' — is an effective escalation. The rewatch value is thematic: this sets up the Troy/Abed fracture that runs through the season.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, Britta, you've got some real seduction skills. I bet you could seduce just about anybody.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's incredibly sexist and objectifying.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? I was giving you a compliment!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, you should rephrase it in a way that doesn't reduce women to their sexual appeal. Maybe try: 'You have a compelling personality and interesting perspectives that make you engaging to talk to.'

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Fine. Britta, you're not bad-looking for a woman with your kind of attitude problem.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Maybe the two of you made out, and then you forgot about her.' Jeff: 'Annie, that's what you think of me? I don't make out with forgettable women.'
jokes.setup: Annie is speculating about why Kim might hate Jeff
jokes.punchline: Jeff's defense of himself — 'I don't make out with forgettable women' — is not actually a defense; it implies he makes out with many women, just only memorable ones. The narcissism of the defense is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Nicely layered character joke. Jeff genuinely believes this is a good defense. The audience hears it as a confession. The gap between his self-perception and reality is precisely Jeff's character arc, compressed into one line. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, before you congratulate me... I need to tell you something. I may have gotten a little too close to the target. Emotionally close.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh no. Britta, no.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I think I have feelings for him.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's the espionage! It happens to the best of us.

jokes.text: They find out Kim is 'no longer with us.' 'She died two weeks ago.' Jeff and Annie react with shock. The person adds: 'Sorry to drop that on you and run, but there's a rally for Garrett.' 'But we saved him.' 'Did we?'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to find Kim to apologize; they're told she 'is no longer with us'
jokes.punchline: The 'rally for Garrett' callback drops the Kim bombshell and immediately pivots to Garrett — but 'Did we?' reintroduces doubt about whether Garrett was actually saved, extending the earlier gag
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — delivers a dramatic beat (Kim's death) and two separate comedy beats in rapid succession. The 'Did we?' callback to the Garrett gag is well-timed, using the comedic rhythm to process the shocking news. The pivot from death to Garrett rally is classically Community: emotional whiplash used for comedic effect.

jokes.text: Britta approaches the Subway counter with hostility: 'What's it to you, meat pusher?' Subway responds: 'Sounds like you might be a vegetarian.' Then suggests the Veggie Delite.
jokes.setup: Britta is approaching Subway with confrontational political hostility
jokes.punchline: Subway immediately and accurately identifies her as a vegetarian and pivots to a sales pitch — his corporate programming turns her aggression into a sales opportunity instantly
jokes.explanation: Good role reversal — Britta's planned righteous confrontation is immediately neutralized by Subway's corporate-trained helpfulness. 'Meat pusher' is a good Britta line. The irony is that his ability to read and service her needs is exactly what makes the corpohumanization horror real.

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: I had a dream last night. A three-legged dog was negotiating peace in the Middle East.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's actually a powerful metaphor for overcoming—

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: Then a one-eyed cat was mediating trade disputes between nations.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: See, disability doesn't define—

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: A deaf gerbil successfully negotiated the Iran nuclear deal.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's kind of beautiful when you think about—

dialogue.speaker: Subway
dialogue.line: And a paraplegic hamster just completely rejected your entire point of view.

jokes.text: Britta: 'You should try reading Orwell's 1984.' Subway: 'I have. It's a great book. It really awakened me in High School. I think kids should be forced to read it.' Britta: 'Me too. Anyway, you're living it.'
jokes.setup: Britta recommends 1984 as a slam, expecting Subway to be ignorant of or hostile to it
jokes.punchline: Subway enthusiastically agrees it's great and says kids should be 'forced to read it' — a sincere statement that is also darkly ironic given that he is literally living in a totalitarian corporate system. Britta's 'Anyway, you're living it' is the button.
jokes.explanation: Smart satirical comedy. The twist is that Subway is fully self-aware about the literature that critiques his existence, and can even enthusiastically endorse it, while remaining trapped in the system. 'Anyway, you're living it' is an excellent button — Britta's attempt at a cultural slam becomes genuine pathos. This conversation seeds the Britta/Subway romance effectively while being genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Laybourne played me like a fiddle. I went from being Abed's sidekick to being his underkick.

jokes.text: An elderly student named Harry is encountered. Subway: 'Eat these tater tots, Harry. For what it's worth, I think you might see more than all of us.'
jokes.setup: An older student appears, apparently visually impaired ('My eyesight ain't what it used to be')
jokes.punchline: Subway treats this clearly confused old man with sincere reverence as a sage figure — 'you might see more than all of us' — while giving him tater tots. The non-sequitur depth is very funny.
jokes.explanation: Charming and strange. Subway dispensing tater tots and quasi-philosophical compliments to a confused old man is an oddly touching absurdist beat. It also characterizes Subway as genuinely sweet, which makes his eventual firing more effective.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done! You're a butt-licker!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, that doesn't even make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's what you are!

jokes.text: Pierce to Britta after the Subway interaction: 'Top-notch whoresmanship, Britta.' Then: 'Sorry. Whoreswomanship. Forgot it was the '90s.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is congratulating Britta on her flirting with Subway as part of the espionage plan
jokes.punchline: He invents 'whoresmanship,' then corrects himself to 'whoreswomanship' — but the correction reveals that he thinks making it gender-neutral is the only problematic part of the original word. 'Forgot it was the '90s' implies he lives in some pre-enlightenment period.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce joke — he attempts a correction to be more sensitive but the correction is itself offensive (inventing 'whoreswomanship' as a feminist upgrade). 'Forgot it was the '90s' implies the '90s are his reference point for progressive politics, which is very funny and character-specific. The neologism 'whoresmanship'/'whoreswomanship' has genuine comic invention.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm sorry you feel that way.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not an apology, that's a magical spell to make me disappear.

jokes.text: Britta: 'That's me, the girl who's going to destroy the big sandwich company with the dreamy eyes.'
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce are congratulating Britta on her espionage mission
jokes.punchline: Britta involuntarily adds 'with the dreamy eyes' to her description of Subway — revealing her romantic susceptibility even as she's supposed to be a cold corporate spy
jokes.explanation: Economical character comedy. The addition of 'with the dreamy eyes' in a moment of self-betrayal tells the audience everything about where this storyline is going while being funny on its own. Shirley and Pierce's triumphant 'We did it!' — which immediately follows a line that signals the opposite — is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: I missed out on pillow access, and now I'm comparing it to a financial opportunity from decades ago.

jokes.text: Subway and Britta are reading 1984 together. He's circled the passage 'She had become a physical necessity.' Britta notes the circled passage; Subway: 'I can't say that I did.'
jokes.setup: They're having a surprisingly deep connection over a book Subway has circled
jokes.punchline: His denial that he circled it — delivered while clearly having circled it and while Britta is holding evidence — is both a corporate-programmed deflection and a romantic comedy beat. The passage itself ('physical necessity') foreshadows everything.
jokes.explanation: Good layered joke. The denial is simultaneously a corporate reflex (he can't admit to romantic feelings) and a terrible lie (Britta is holding the circled book). The passage from 1984 is thematically loaded — it'll be echoed when Britta later describes Subway as her 'physical necessity.' Good rewatch value for how much it sets up.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'll create the perfect woman. A Britta, but without all the Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: She'll have Britta's body, but my intelligence downloading directly into her brain.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We'll call her Britta 2.0. The first model was just a prototype that gained sentience and became annoying.

jokes.text: Subway reveals his dream: 'I want to run a nonprofit shelter for handicapped animals. Dogs with wheels for hind legs. Deaf hamsters.' Britta: 'One-eyed cats?' Subway: 'Well, they weren't on the top of my list, but sure.'
jokes.setup: Britta asks Subway what his dream is after his corporate sentence is served
jokes.punchline: He wants to open a handicapped animal shelter — a completely pure, wholesome dream — but Britta tries to participate with 'one-eyed cats,' and he gently but specifically clarifies they weren't a priority. The specificity of his dream list (wheeled dogs, deaf hamsters) is the main joke.
jokes.explanation: Funny and touching at the same time. The specificity of 'dogs with wheels for hind legs' and 'deaf hamsters' (not just 'disabled animals' but specific beloved subsets) characterizes Subway as genuinely sweet. Britta's attempt to contribute ('one-eyed cats?') and Subway's precise but polite correction is an unexpected comic beat that humanizes both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Here, take this invisible ink pen. For your spy work.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Thanks, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: *drinks the ink*

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's invisible, right? So it won't show up on my teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's not— Britta, you look terrible.

jokes.text: Troy confronts Abed: 'Why do I always have to be your Reggie?' After Abed gives permission to make a blanket fort: 'Thank you.' Abed: 'Just don't make it part of my pillow fort.' Troy: 'Fine. I'll start it somewhere else. Have fun stacking pillows like a baby.'
jokes.setup: Troy has absorbed Laybourne's Inspector/Reggie analogy and is now asserting independence
jokes.punchline: After a sincere emotional moment, the resolution is Troy calling Abed's artistic project 'stacking pillows like a baby' — a childish insult that also accurately describes what Abed is doing, delivered as Troy storms off
jokes.explanation: The Troy/Abed fracture is the episode's most emotionally resonant plot, and this moment crystallizes it with 'stacking pillows like a baby.' The insult is both petty (it's literally what fort-building is) and a child's taunt — perfect for the show's exploration of adult friendships through childlike activities. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Britta, listen. When you're undercover, the key is to blend in. You need to change your appearance completely.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Maybe lose some weight, get some work done on your face. You know, the usual stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Pierce!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, you're not exactly helping the cause looking like... well, like you.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Fine. I'll start it somewhere else. Have fun stacking pillows like a baby.'
jokes.setup: Troy storms off after being told his fort can't connect to Abed's
jokes.punchline: 'Stacking pillows like a baby' is a genuinely funny insult — both specific to the activity and completely the wrong register for the intensity Troy's trying to project
jokes.explanation: Very Troy — trying to be cutting and landing on something that's both mean and sort of sweet. 'Like a baby' is the right level of absurd for a grown man fighting about pillow forts.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not just breaking records, I'm joining an elite community of record holders. We have secret meetings in a hidden library where we discuss our achievements over imported cheese and wine.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: There's a handshake. A very complicated handshake. It takes forty-five minutes to learn.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And once a year, we gather under the full moon to renew our vows as record holders. We wear special robes. Mine is burgundy.

jokes.text: Jeff is lying on campus furniture. Annie: 'Is it about this Kim girl?' Jeff: 'She is someone who died thinking I was a dick. I can never apologize. I can never change her mind. That makes me a dick forever.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is in existential distress about Kim's death
jokes.punchline: His entire moral crisis is framed in terms of his reputation — not 'I hurt someone' but 'I'm a dick forever.' The existential permanence of 'a dick forever' is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Jeff's narcissism reframes genuine guilt as a reputation problem. 'A dick forever' has a nice ring. The scene is primarily dramatic but has this comedic undercurrent of Jeff's self-centeredness even in his most sincere moments.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is it. Fort Hawthorne is under attack. All personnel must evacuate immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Abed, come on!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, Troy. There's no room for friendship in wartime.

dialogue.speaker: Magnitude
dialogue.line: POP POP!

jokes.text: Annie: 'You think that's what an apology is? A spell you cast on another person to make them forgive you? Apologies are opportunities to admit your own mistakes.' Then: 'Apologize to her locker.'
jokes.setup: Jeff says he can't apologize because Kim is dead
jokes.punchline: Annie delivers a sincere monologue about the nature of apology, then completely undercuts the gravity with the entirely practical instruction to 'apologize to her locker.' The bathos is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character moments. Annie's ability to be both genuinely wise and completely literal-minded is a core character trait, and 'apologize to her locker' is a perfect expression of it. The transition from philosophical insight to immediate practical instruction is funny precisely because she means it completely. Character integration is excellent — only Annie would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It was a pleasure to burn.

jokes.text: Leonard appears. Annie: 'Leonard, what are you doing?' Leonard: 'Abed's fort needs pillows.' Annie: 'But I was going to lie there.' Leonard: 'I was going to invest in IBM in 1952, but life is full of disappointments.'
jokes.setup: Annie is about to relax on the pillows Leonard is now collecting for the fort
jokes.punchline: Leonard's response — a deadpan parallel between Annie's minor inconvenience and his failure to invest in IBM in 1952 — implies he has been nursing this regret for 60+ years AND that he treats both as equivalent disappointments
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes and among Leonard's best moments. The structure is immaculate: complaint about a trivial inconvenience → elderly person's specific, historically grounded, decades-old regret → 'life is full of disappointments' as a philosophy that collapses 60 years of financial regret and Annie's pillow inconvenience into the same emotional register. The specificity of 'IBM in 1952' (versus a generic 'investment') is what makes it exceptional. High quotability. Comparable to and arguably exceeding the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Pierce to Britta: 'I think you're falling for him.' Britta: 'I am not. Who do you think I am? I lived in New York.' Pierce: 'You never lived anywhere. You're a weapon designed for sex. You only think you lived in New York because I implanted your memories.'
jokes.setup: Pierce accuses Britta of falling for Subway
jokes.punchline: Pierce escalates from skepticism to a full Blade Runner/Total Recall-style conspiracy claim that he implanted Britta's memories of living in New York. 'A weapon designed for sex' is an unexpected mid-sentence pivot.
jokes.explanation: One of Pierce's wildest escalations. 'A weapon designed for sex' is a memorably bizarre insult/compliment hybrid. The memory implantation claim is pure absurdism that makes no internal sense yet fits Pierce's grandiosity. High originality because the sci-fi conspiracy turn is completely unpredictable. The line 'You never lived anywhere' as a prelude to the memory implant reveal is good structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Kim
dialogue.line: I wrote that note because you assumed I was a woman.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No, I didn't—

dialogue.speaker: Kim
dialogue.line: You called me 'she' in your email. My name is Kim, and you defaulted to female. That's the first layer of your thoughtlessness.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I apologize, I just—

dialogue.speaker: Kim
dialogue.line: The second layer is that you didn't even bother to check. You just sent it off. The third layer is that you're now trying to smooth this over with charm instead of actually listening.

jokes.text: Pierce produces a pen that is also a microphone, also a miniflask. 'Did you just drink ink?'
jokes.setup: Pierce presents Britta with a spy pen microphone for her mission
jokes.punchline: The pen is apparently also a flask, and Pierce apparently just drank from it — meaning he drank ink
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy beat. The pen-as-flask is a spy parody detail, and Pierce drinking from it immediately (accidentally? intentionally?) is a great button. 'Did you just drink ink?' lands well. The escalating functionality of the pen (microphone → flask → he drinks from it) is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Kim
dialogue.line: Did you know that 87% of people named Kim are confused about their own gender at least once a week? It's true. I read it somewhere.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'And for God's sakes, slap some life on those dead lips.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is briefing Britta on her mission
jokes.punchline: The instruction to 'slap some life on those dead lips' is an aggressive, backhanded comment about Britta's appearance disguised as mission prep
jokes.explanation: Solid Pierce cringe comedy — the casual insult embedded in mission instructions is very him. 'Dead lips' is a funny specific choice. Not his sharpest line but it maintains the Pierce/Britta dynamic effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: My teaching method is proven effective and research-backed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, that's great. Very earnest. But let's be honest - you're about as inspiring as a TPS report written in crayon.

jokes.text: Troy on potential Guinness record perks: 'we might be meeting those two fat guys on motorcycles and being fitted for a beard of bees.'
jokes.setup: Troy is envisioning the benefits of a Guinness world record
jokes.punchline: 'Being fitted for a beard of bees' — Troy imagines Guinness record achievement as a world where you are costumed in bees, presented as a standard professional perk
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original absurdism. 'Beard of bees' is a Guinness record staple (there are real bee beard records), but Troy presenting it as a fitting — something you're 'fitted' for, like a suit — is an unexpected specific verb choice that elevates it. The casualness of the vision is very Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I don't know if I can do this.

dialogue.speaker: The Inspector
dialogue.line: You must. Art is the crystalline expression of the human condition, a mirror held up to society's face. To compromise it is to betray not merely yourself, but the very essence of what makes us sentient beings capable of transcendence.

jokes.text: Garrett: 'Abed's pillow fort is the only thing standing in our way.' Dean: 'Is there a way we can connect them?' Troy: 'You can't connect the blanket fort to the pillow fort and still call it a pillow fort.' Abed: 'Even if you could, I'd rather see my work destroyed than compromise it.'
jokes.setup: The Dean tries to broker a simple compromise between the two forts
jokes.punchline: Abed's declaration that he'd rather see his work destroyed than compromised is delivered with complete sincerity about a pillow fort — an absurd application of artistic integrity
jokes.explanation: Abed's artistic absolutism applied to a pillow fort is a perfect character joke — he is functionally indistinguishable in this speech from an auteur director refusing studio notes. Character integration is very high. The gap between the grandeur of the declaration and the subject matter (pillows) is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, come back! Your speech was so inspiring!

dialogue.speaker: Mysterious Figure
dialogue.line: I appreciate that, but I need to crawl away now. I'm having some personal issues.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton: 'Great, Abed will destroy his pillow fort, and Troy will expand his blanket fort into the space. Everyone wins.' Then catches himself: 'Except Abed, but you know, not everyone can win.'
jokes.setup: The Dean has just proposed a 'compromise' that entirely benefits Troy
jokes.punchline: 'Except Abed, but you know, not everyone can win' — the Dean catches the flaw in his own framing and immediately accepts it without moral qualm
jokes.explanation: Good Dean Pelton moment — his institutional authority combined with complete disregard for fairness is a consistent character note. The self-correction that isn't actually a correction is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: I pride myself on being progressive and socially conscious. I've donated to NPR, I drive a Prius, I use the correct pronouns...

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: But nothing prepared me for this. My entire value system is collapsing.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Is that what you want, Troy? For me to destroy my pillow fort so you can set your record?' Troy: 'It is.' Magnitude: 'Evacuate Fort Abed and prepare for self-destruct.' Abed: 'Sir?' Magnitude: 'Do it. We're done here. Pop pop, Captain.'
jokes.setup: The fort conflict has reached a dramatic climax; Abed asks if Troy really wants him to destroy his work
jokes.punchline: Magnitude — a character who exists only to say 'Pop pop' — arrives, says 'Pop pop, Captain,' salutes, and deploys. His participation in the military-operation framing of the fort conflict, complete with rank, is perfect absurdism.
jokes.explanation: Magnitude's deployment as military operator of the fort deconstruction is excellent character comedy — a one-note character used for maximum effect in one beat. 'Pop pop, Captain' is a variation on his catchphrase that gains gravity from the military context. Good economy — Magnitude appears, delivers, exits.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done here. I'm walking out that door and I'm never coming back.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: And there's nothing any of you can do to stop me.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: Wait, has anyone seen where I put my jacket?

jokes.text: Britta admits to Subway that she was sent to plant a bug on him, then declares: 'Our values, our identities... they mean nothing to me now. Only the primal remains. To me, you are simply a physical necessity.'
jokes.setup: Britta is confessing and pivoting to romance instead of espionage
jokes.punchline: 'Physical necessity' is the exact phrase from the 1984 passage they read together earlier — Britta has become the character in the book, fulfilling the foreshadowing. Using Orwell as a seduction text while literally living inside the corporate dystopia it describes is rich irony.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback payoff — the circled 1984 passage has been seeded carefully and now Britta deploys it as a seduction line, fully embodying what the passage describes. The irony that she's using anti-corporate dystopian literature as romantic language in a corporate-human seduction is multi-layered. Good structural craft.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: This conversation is over. I'm leaving.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: Could someone help me with my jacket?

jokes.text: Pierce watches from outside the pillow fort as Britta and Subway make out: 'No, this is wrong, Pierce. I just wanted to open a sandwich shop. I did not sign up for this.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has been orchestrating the espionage plan; now he's watching it go off the rails romantically
jokes.punchline: Shirley's protest 'I just wanted to open a sandwich shop' perfectly refocuses the entire subplot — the corporate satire and sexual espionage were always, at their core, about Shirley wanting to sell sandwiches
jokes.explanation: Good bathos — the reduction of a complicated corporate espionage/romance plot to 'I just wanted to open a sandwich shop' perfectly deflates the whole subplot. Shirley's grounded ordinariness is her best character note.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Executive
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget it. I'm not leaving. I'm going to process my trauma right here, right now, in front of all of you.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'You don't want to get your hands dirty, fine. I will. Nice knowing you, Subway. If that is your real name.'
jokes.setup: Shirley refuses to continue with the spy plan; Pierce declares he'll handle it
jokes.punchline: 'Nice knowing you, Subway. If that is your real name.' — after the entire episode has established that 'Subway' IS in fact his real (legal) name, Pierce affects spy-movie skepticism about the alias
jokes.explanation: Smart callback. The whole episode has established that Subway is his actual legal name. Pierce performing spy-movie doubt about an alias that is definitively NOT an alias is a good ironic reversal. Very economical — the line lands in a single breath.

jokes.text: Jeff's locker apology to Kim. Emotional speech. Then: 'I am. And I do. I'm Kim.' Jeff: 'What? You said Kim was dead.' Kim: 'Because you never remember who I am.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has been told Kim is dead; he delivers a sincere apology to her locker
jokes.punchline: Kim is alive and was listening. 'Kim' is not a dead girl — he's a living man who faked his own death-by-proxy to hurt Jeff the way Jeff hurt him
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural moments. The misdirection was set up carefully — 'she,' 'girl's name,' the hat on the locker — and the reveal works dramatically and comedically. The irony that the joke about Jeff's obliviousness has been a live performance is elegant. The structure of Jeff apologizing to a locker while the person is standing next to him is a great visual setup.

dialogue.speaker: New Subway
dialogue.line: We're excited to bring a fresh, innovative dining experience to Greendale. Our new paradigm focuses on synergistic engagement with our key demographics.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That sounds great.

dialogue.speaker: New Subway
dialogue.line: We've also streamlined our touch-points to maximize customer satisfaction metrics. Of course, we take all allegations of non-consensual contact very seriously and have implemented a robust reporting infrastructure.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, what?

jokes.text: Kim explains: 'First year, we hung out like ten times. And each time, you introduced yourself to me.' Then: 'And you still assume from my name that I am a girl.'
jokes.setup: Kim is explaining the full scope of Jeff's obliviousness
jokes.punchline: Jeff forgot Kim ten times, never learned his name, AND assumed from the name that Kim was a woman — a triple failure of basic human acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: Good escalating indictment of Jeff's narcissism. The escalation — forgot him ten times, assumed female gender from name — lands each beat cleanly. '16% of all people named Kim are men' is a funny specific statistic that Kim has clearly researched.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Wait, who am I fighting for again?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Your own fort!

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Right, right. But which one is mine? I've built so many identities, I can't remember which fort represents the real Star-Burns.

jokes.text: Kim: 'I had no choice but to make up that awesome story about a dead chick to hurt you like you hurt me.'
jokes.setup: Kim is explaining his revenge scheme
jokes.punchline: 'That awesome story about a dead chick' — Kim is completely self-satisfied with his own deception, calling it 'awesome' as if reviewing a heist film
jokes.explanation: Kim's self-congratulation ('awesome story') is a good character note — his petty revenge has been deeply satisfying to him. 'Dead chick' as a summary of his elaborate deception is funny in its bluntness.

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: You know, I've been called a lot of things. Cold-hearted, manipulative, calculating...

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.line: Sir, the air conditioning in your office—

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: Yes, yes, I like it arctic. Keeps people on their toes. Speaking of which, I suppose you could say I run a pretty cold-blooded operation around here.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.line: You mean the thermostat is set to 62 degrees?

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: Exactly. Cold-blooded. Now get me another yogurt.

jokes.text: Jeff apologizes. Kim: 'Do you know how long I've waited to hear you say that?'
jokes.setup: Jeff finally says Kim's name correctly
jokes.punchline: Kim's sincere emotional relief at simply being remembered — 'Do you know how long I've waited to hear you say that?' — played completely straight as a profound moment, is both touching and funny
jokes.explanation: Effective bathos — the grand romantic/dramatic payoff is Jeff simply saying someone's name correctly. The disproportionate emotional weight Kim places on this tiny act is funny and a little sad.

jokes.text: Annie, upon meeting Kim: 'I thought I was representing the sisterhood.' Kim turns out to be a man. Annie is embarrassed.
jokes.setup: Annie had been invested in the Kim storyline as a feminist cause, coaching Jeff to apologize to 'the girls he dominates'
jokes.punchline: Kim is a man. Annie's feminist advocacy was entirely misdirected.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on Annie's character arc in the subplot. Her earnest feminist advocacy has been misdirected the whole time, and 'I thought I was representing the sisterhood' acknowledges the absurdity. The joke works because Annie's investment was genuine, not cynical.

jokes.text: Annie on her behavior toward Kim: 'Not to waste your energy on some weird, cloying, hypersensitive stalker with a girl's name.' Kim: 'Hey! You are really mean.' Annie: 'Put it in a letter, Jane Austen.'
jokes.setup: Annie has been scolding Jeff and is now fully pivoting to dismiss Kim after her feminist framing collapsed
jokes.punchline: 'Put it in a letter, Jane Austen' — Annie weaponizes Kim's letter-writing as a gendered insult, while also making a literary reference that calls him old-fashioned. The speed of the turn from feminist advocacy to 'you're a stalker' is the cringe joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Annie line and one of the episode's most quotable moments. 'Put it in a letter, Jane Austen' is a great insult — it's specific, it weaponizes the form of communication Kim used to wrong Jeff, and 'Jane Austen' as a dismissive literary put-down is clever. The snap from feminist ally to catty dismissal is a good character subversion. High quotability.

jokes.text: Abed gives the order: 'Prepare to initiate Protocol Omega.' Then: 'Good-bye, pillow fort. You were a beautiful dream.' Next: 'More than a dream. It's here.'
jokes.setup: Abed has agreed to destroy the pillow fort and is performing the ceremony of its destruction
jokes.punchline: 'Protocol Omega' and the genuine grief of 'You were a beautiful dream' applied to a pillow fort is Abed treating the mundane as sacred — his flattest affect for his most sincere emotions. Then 'More than a dream. It's here.' undercuts even the grief with Abed's literalism.
jokes.explanation: Very strong Abed character work. 'Protocol Omega' as the name for pillow fort demolition is excellent (military language for a children's activity), and the elegiac 'You were a beautiful dream' is sincere Abed — he genuinely mourns the fort. The final 'More than a dream. It's here.' — a reflexive correction because the fort literally exists — is Abed's literalism as philosophy. Character integration is as high as it gets.

jokes.text: Vice Dean Laybourne appears in the fort: 'Someone who understands dedication to craftsmanship in the face of mediocrity. This world is run by the unremarkables. Don't do what you always do, Abed. Don't corrupt the host to pacify the parasites.'
jokes.setup: Abed is about to destroy his fort; a mysterious figure appears
jokes.punchline: The Vice Dean's grandiose speech about craftsmanship and mediocrity is delivered with absolute seriousness about a PILLOW FORT — the gap between the register of the speech and its subject is the comedy
jokes.explanation: Laybourne's manipulation is delivered as genuine philosophical insight, which makes him both more sinister and funnier. 'Don't corrupt the host to pacify the parasites' is a genuinely memorable phrase deployed for pillow fort politics. The absurdity of the speech's grandeur is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: Laybourne: 'What if it fell to the Reggies of the world to keep up with the inspectors, or perish?' Then: 'Now please turn your head while I crawl away. I'm going through some stuff right now. I'm very insecure.'
jokes.setup: Laybourne has delivered his grandiose speech and needs to exit dramatically from inside a pillow fort
jokes.punchline: He has to physically crawl out, which requires Abed to look away. 'I'm going through some stuff right now. I'm very insecure.' — the callback to his earlier deflection ('going through some stuff'), but now deployed as physical comedy and self-aware vulnerability
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest beats. Laybourne's menacing speech is completely deflated by the physical reality of having to crawl out of a pillow fort. His request for privacy while crawling ('please turn your head') and the double-down with 'I'm very insecure' is a perfect combination of physical comedy and character work. The callback to 'going through some stuff' gains emotional depth — it's the third time he's said it, and each time the insecurity becomes more visible. High rewatch value.

jokes.text: Pierce to Britta: 'You had sex with Subway, and I recorded it.' Then shows what appears to be video. Subway's rep: 'You know what, I'm going to let this one slide.' Then he sees something: 'Th... is this what I think it is?'
jokes.setup: Pierce has used his recording to try to destroy Subway through his corporate handlers
jokes.punchline: The rep initially waves off the sexual content as 'letting this one slide' — implying this happens with some regularity — but then sees something in the recording that escalates beyond their tolerance
jokes.explanation: Good cringe escalation. The 'I'll let this one slide' implies that corpohumanoid sex scandals are a known HR issue. The unseen escalating content on the recording is funnier than anything that could be described.

jokes.text: Corporate rep reacts to the recording: 'That got unhealthy real quick. That... okay, that's weird. That is well out of the mainstream. You know, I was raised in the Bay Area, but I'm a father now.'
jokes.setup: The corporate rep is watching Pierce's recording of Britta and Subway
jokes.punchline: His commentary escalates — 'unhealthy,' then 'weird,' then 'well out of the mainstream' — culminating in his personal biography ('Bay Area, but I'm a father now') as a way of establishing his liberal but limited tolerance
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best escalation jokes. The progression is perfect: each descriptor is worse than the last, and then the pivot to personal testimony ('Bay Area, but I'm a father now') is the detonation. This is an excellent character type — the progressive who has his limits — compressed into two sentences. 'Bay Area, but I'm a father now' is immediately quotable and captures a very specific demographic stance perfectly. The unseen act is funnier for not being described.

jokes.text: Corporate rep to Subway: 'Subway cannot stand for that, and frankly, Rick, I'm surprised you did.' Subway: 'My name is Subway.' Rep: 'Not anymore. The bread is stale.'
jokes.setup: The corporate rep is about to fire Subway/Rick
jokes.punchline: 'The bread is stale' — using Subway's own slogan language ('Eat Fresh') as the termination code is a perfect piece of corporate satire. The loss of identity — his name, his purpose — delivered through sandwich freshness metaphor is simultaneously funny and genuinely dark.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a strong candidate for its standout moment. The setup is perfect — Subway insists on his corporate name as his only identity — and 'The bread is stale' as the termination phrase is a masterclass in satirical economy. It inverts 'Eat Fresh' to signal the end of his corporate personhood. The horror that someone can have their identity revoked with a food freshness metaphor is both funny and genuinely unsettling. High on every dimension. Comparable to and arguably exceeding the 8.0 reference anchor.

jokes.text: Subway reacts to being fired: 'No! No!' Britta: 'Subway, I love you!' Subway's corporate supervisor: 'Shut up.' Britta watches Subway be escorted away.
jokes.setup: Subway is being terminated and dragged away
jokes.punchline: Britta's desperate 'I love you!' to a corporate-branded human being she met 24 hours ago, followed by his handler's flat 'Shut up,' is perfect cringe comedy — the romance plot deflated by corporate HR in one word
jokes.explanation: 'Shut up' as the response to 'I love you' is brutal economy. The corporate supervisor's complete disregard for Britta's feelings is the satirical point (corporations don't care about human feeling) but also just very funny deflation. Good economy in the button.

jokes.text: Pierce, after the entire scene, is standing next to a coat rack. He asks people to hand him his jacket repeatedly, specifying 'It's right over there on the coatrack next to the door. If somebody could just hand it to me, that would be great.' No one helps.
jokes.setup: Everyone else has reacted to the dramatic Subway termination
jokes.punchline: Pierce is unable to retrieve his own jacket from two feet away and makes increasingly specific requests that everyone ignores — culminating in him deciding not to leave at all out of spite
jokes.explanation: Underrated Pierce physical gag. The escalating specificity of his jacket directions ('right over there, next to the door') as everyone ignores him is a good sustained awkward comedy beat. His final decision not to leave — 'Now I'm just going to sit for a while and focus on how unacceptable today was' — is a perfect Pierce line.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I guess I'm confused. Why don't you just grab it on your way out the door...' / Nobody hands it to him / 'You know what? Now I'm not leaving. Now I'm just going to sit for a while and focus on how unacceptable today was.'
jokes.setup: Pierce can't get anyone to hand him his jacket and is being questioned on why he doesn't just grab it himself
jokes.punchline: He refuses to exit without the jacket and declares he's staying to 'focus on how unacceptable today was' — a toddler-level tantrum in the aftermath of his own villainous scheme
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Pierce having the most childish possible response to a minor logistical problem — refusing to leave, holding a sit-in of personal grievance — is perfect character work. 'Focus on how unacceptable today was' is a great line. This whole jacket sequence is a gem.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Now I'm just going to sit for a while and focus on how unacceptable today was.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has decided not to leave because no one handed him his jacket
jokes.punchline: He announces his plan to sit and 'focus on how unacceptable today was' — as if 'focusing on unacceptableness' is a recognized therapeutic practice
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce line. 'Focus on how unacceptable today was' is a perfect Pierce attitude — aggrieved, passive, and self-righteous simultaneously. The word 'focus' implying active mental effort on grievance nursing is very funny. High quotability, strong economy. One of Pierce's best moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Annie apologizes to Jeff for her behavior with Kim. Jeff: 'Mm.' Annie: 'Who's Kim?'
jokes.setup: Annie is delivering a sincere apology about gender roles and her treatment of Kim
jokes.punchline: Jeff has already moved on and forgotten Kim — immediately proving Kim's original complaint about Jeff's obliviousness is universal, and showing Jeff hasn't changed at all
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most structurally elegant jokes. In two words ('Who's Kim?'), Jeff completely undermines the entire emotional arc he just went through. The lesson has not been learned. The apology was not transformative. This is the character-specific punchline the entire Kim subplot was building toward. Economy is near-perfect — nine words to close a 15-minute subplot with a single devastating joke. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably exceeding it in structural elegance.

jokes.text: New Subway student appears: 'Subway!' / Britta: 'Oh, I'm sorry, I thought you were someone else.' / New Subway: 'Britta, you silly. It is me, Subway.' — it is literally a different person with the same corporate identity
jokes.setup: Britta is grieving the loss of Subway; a new student who is also named Subway appears
jokes.punchline: The corporation has simply replaced the previous Subway with a new human, and the new one insists he IS Subway — the brand identity is transferable across bodies
jokes.explanation: Excellent satirical payoff on the corpohumanization premise. The corporation treating human identity as interchangeable corporate assets — and the new Subway sincerely claiming to be the same Subway — is a sharp joke about how corporations view their employees. 'Britta, you silly. It is me, Subway' is delivered with complete earnestness. Very high originality and earned comedy scores.

jokes.text: Britta weeping: 'Corporate America has destroyed love.' Pierce/someone: 'Again?' Britta: 'Subway!' — then looks at a stranger: 'Oh, I'm sorry, I thought you were someone else.'
jokes.setup: Britta is having a breakdown over Subway's termination
